examTechnique.papers: Three papers × 1 h 30 min, 80 marks each. Paper 1 is non-calculator; Papers 2 & 3 allow a calculator. Any topic can appear on any paper — content is mixed.
examTechnique.timing: 80 marks in 90 minutes is just over one minute per mark. A 5-mark question deserves about 6 minutes, not 15. If stuck after two minutes, write anything true (a formula, a sketch, an inequality) and move on; return in the last 15 minutes. Never leave a multi-mark question blank.

markTypes.meaning: Method mark — a correct method, even if the arithmetic later fails. Write the method so a stranger can follow it.
Accuracy mark — depends on the method. Follow-through (ft) is often allowed after an earlier slip.
Independent mark — a correct value or statement on its own.
Communication — correct notation, units, and named reasons in geometry and proof.

commandWords.meaning: Give a numerical or algebraic answer. Show method.
Arrive at the given result. Do not use the result at the start.
A short sentence or a named theorem. Not a number alone.
Transformations: type + all parameters. Correlation: strength + direction + context.
Round first (usually 1 s.f.), then calculate. Do not give an exact calculator value.
Use the previous result. A new method may score zero.
Leave in terms of π, √, or a fraction. Do not write a rounded decimal.

examTechnique.exactValues: sin 0=0, sin 30=½, sin 45=√2/2, sin 60=√3/2, sin 90=1.  cos 0=1, cos 30=√3/2, cos 45=√2/2, cos 60=½, cos 90=0.  tan 0=0, tan 30=1/√3, tan 45=1, tan 60=√3. These appear on non-calculator papers every year.
lastFiveMinutes: Check a length is not negative.
Check an angle in a triangle is less than 180°.
Check you answered the actual question — sometimes part (b) asks for the difference, not the value you just found.

strands.name: Number
strands.note: Number underpins every other strand. On Foundation it is a quarter of the marks. Practise without a calculator every week.

subtopics.title: Ordering; four operations; negatives
subtopics.method: BIDMAS / BODMAS sets the order: Brackets, Indices, Division and Multiplication (left to right), Addition and Subtraction (left to right). Two minuses make a plus: 3 − (−5) = 8. Multiplying or dividing two negatives gives a positive; a single negative in a product makes it negative. Order fractions and decimals by place value or by converting to a common form.
tips: Practise the four operations without a calculator at least weekly.
Line up decimal points when adding or subtracting.

subtopics.title: Factors, multiples, primes, HCF & LCM
subtopics.method: Prime numbers have exactly two factors (1 and themselves); 1 is not prime. Prime factorisation writes a number as a product of primes in index form: 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5. HCF: take the lowest power of each shared prime. LCM: take the highest power of every prime that appears. These are often set in worded contexts (tiling, bus timetables, packing).
tips: Know square numbers to 15² = 225 and cubes to 10³ = 1000.
Method — HCF/LCM via primes: factor trees → index form → HCF = lowest shared powers, LCM = highest powers of all.

subtopics.title: Fractions: four operations, mixed numbers
subtopics.method: Equivalent fractions by multiplying or dividing numerator and denominator by the same number — always cancel before multiplying. Add/subtract: common denominator. Multiply: numerators together, denominators together. Divide: keep, change, flip (multiply by the reciprocal). Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions first.
tips: Cancelling early prevents large, messy numbers.

subtopics.title: FDP conversions; percentages of amounts; increase/decrease
subtopics.method: Always convert the percentage to a decimal multiplier. Increase of 12% → × 1.12. Decrease of 15% → × 0.85. Find 17% of 80 → 80 × 0.17. Express 18 as a percentage of 24 → (18 ÷ 24) × 100 = 75%.
tips: Worked template — % increase/decrease: 1) write the multiplier, 2) multiply, 3) if 'how much more' subtract original from new, 4) units.

subtopics.title: Reverse percentages; interest; growth & decay
formulae: Compound interest / growth: final = original × (1 + r/100)ⁿ
subtopics.method: Reverse percentages: the given amount is already the result after a change. A sale price of £68 at 15% off is 85% of the original, so original = 68 ÷ 0.85. Never add or subtract the percentage of the new amount — that is the classic trap. Simple interest is on the original principal each year; compound growth/decay uses the power formula. 'Compounded annually for 4 years at 3%' is × (1.03)⁴, not × 1.12.
tips: Worked template — reverse %: 1) identify what 100% represents, 2) write the given value as a % of the original, 3) divide by that multiplier.

subtopics.title: Index laws (including zero and negative)
subtopics.method: Write these laws fluently and apply them one step at a time.

subtopics.title: Standard form calculations
formulae: a × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ a < 10 and n is an integer
subtopics.method: To multiply: multiply the a-parts and add the indices. To divide: divide the a-parts and subtract the indices. Then renormalise if a is no longer between 1 and 10. On calculator papers use the ×10ˣ or EXP key — never type 2.4 × 10 ^ 7 as 2.4 × 10 × 7.

subtopics.title: Rounding, estimation, error intervals & bounds
subtopics.method: Significant figures: count from the first non-zero digit. Decimal places: count from the decimal point. Look at the next digit — 5 or more rounds up. Error interval: a length of 8.3 cm to 1 d.p. means 8.25 ≤ x < 8.35 (≤ on the lower bound, < on the upper). Truncation is different — check the wording. Bounds in calculations: maximum of a sum or product uses both upper bounds; maximum of a quotient uses the upper of the numerator and the lower of the denominator. Write UB and LB explicitly.
tips: Estimate questions: round each value to 1 s.f. first, then calculate.

subtopics.title: Fractional indices; surds; rationalising; recurring decimals
subtopics.method: Fractional indices — do the root first to keep numbers small: 8^(2/3) = (∛8)² = 2² = 4. Surds — simplify by extracting square factors: √50 = √(25×2) = 5√2. Rationalise the denominator: single term × the surd; binomial × the conjugate, e.g. 1/(√5 − 2) × (√5 + 2)/(√5 + 2) = √5 + 2. Recurring decimals → fractions: let x = 0.1̇7̇, multiply by 10 or 100 to line up the repeat, subtract, then divide. Show the algebra — it is an AO2 mark.

strands.name: Algebra
strands.note: On Higher, algebra is the largest single strand and the language of almost every problem-solving question. Keep clean layout: one equals sign per line, aligned, with a short reason where a step is not obvious.

subtopics.title: Simplify, expand & factorise (including DOTS)
formulae: Difference of two squares: a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b)
subtopics.method: Collect like terms (powers of x are not like x): 3x + 5 − x + 2 = 2x + 7. Expand a single bracket: 3(2x − 5) = 6x − 15; watch a negative outside: −2(x − 4) = −2x + 8. Expand double brackets with FOIL or a grid: (x + 3)(x − 7) = x² − 4x − 21. Factorise: always take out the highest common factor first. Trinomials: find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. DOTS: x² − 9 = (x + 3)(x − 3); 4y² − 25 = (2y + 5)(2y − 5).
tips: Triple brackets [H]: expand two first, then multiply by the third.

subtopics.title: Linear equations; inequalities; number lines
subtopics.method: Do the same operation to both sides. Collect unknowns on one side; expand brackets first unless a common factor makes factorising faster. Substitute your answer back as a 10-second check. Inequalities are solved like equations, with one extra rule: if you multiply or divide by a negative, reverse the inequality sign. On a number line use a filled circle for ≤ or ≥, an open circle for < or >.
tips: Quadratic inequalities [H]: sketch the parabola, find roots, then read the region required.

subtopics.title: Rearranging formulae (change the subject)
subtopics.method: Treat the new subject like the 'x' you are solving for and use inverse operations in reverse BIDMAS order. If the new subject appears twice, factorise it out. Example: make x the subject of y = (x + 3)/(x − 1) — multiply both sides by (x − 1), expand, collect x-terms, factorise x, divide.
tips: Worked template: 1) expand if needed, 2) collect subject terms on one side, 3) factorise the subject if it appears twice, 4) divide, 5) check by substituting a number.

subtopics.title: Linear graphs y = mx + c; parallel lines; real-life graphs
formulae: Equation of a straight line: y = mx + c
subtopics.method: m is the gradient (rise/run), c is the y-intercept. Parallel lines have equal gradients. To find the equation from two points: find m, then substitute one point to find c. On real-life graphs the gradient is a rate.
tips: Perpendicular lines [H]: m₁ × m₂ = −1.

subtopics.title: Sequences: linear nth term; special sequences
subtopics.method: Linear (arithmetic): find the common difference d, then adjust the constant so it fits term 1. Recognise square, cube, triangular and Fibonacci-style sequences. Fibonacci-style sequences are defined by a rule relating previous terms — write the next terms, do not force an nth term unless asked.
tips: Quadratic sequences [H]: second differences are constant; the coefficient of n² is (second difference) ÷ 2.

subtopics.title: Quadratic graphs; solving by factorising
subtopics.method: Sketch the parabola (U or ∩); the roots are where y = 0. Solve by factorising: set each bracket equal to 0. Read turning points and intercepts from the graph.
tips: Worked template — quadratic equation: 1) set equal to zero, 2) try factorising, 3) each factor = 0 gives a solution.

subtopics.title: Simultaneous equations (two linear)
subtopics.method: Elimination (make the coefficients of one variable equal, then add or subtract) or substitution. Label the equations clearly. After finding one variable, substitute back — and check in the equation you did not just use.

subtopics.title: Quadratic formula; completing the square; quadratic inequalities
formulae: Completing the square: x² + bx = (x + b/2)² − (b/2)²
subtopics.method: Use the quadratic formula when factorising is messy or impossible over the integers — write the formula first, then substitute (use brackets for negatives). The discriminant b² − 4ac tells you the number of real roots: positive → two, zero → one repeated, negative → none. Completing the square gives turning points and exact form: x² + 6x + 5 = (x + 3)² − 4, minimum −4 at x = −3. Quadratic inequalities: sketch the parabola, find the roots, read the region.

subtopics.title: Linear + quadratic simultaneous; algebraic fractions; functions
subtopics.method: Linear + quadratic: rearrange the linear equation for y (or x), substitute into the quadratic, solve, then find the paired values — these are the intersection points of a line and a curve. Algebraic fractions: factorise everything first, cancel common factors (never cancel terms that are added), use a common denominator to add/subtract. Functions: fg(x) means apply g first, then f; the inverse f⁻¹(x) swaps x and y then rearranges.

subtopics.title: Iteration; proof; circle & tangent; graph transformations
formulae: Equation of a circle centre origin: x² + y² = r²
subtopics.method: Iteration: rearrange into xₙ₊₁ = …, substitute repeatedly, show convergence to the required decimal places. Proof: start from the given expression, use algebra (odd = 2n+1, consecutive = n, n+1, n+2), and finish with a sentence such as 'which is always a multiple of 4'. Do not start from what you are trying to prove. Transformations: y = f(x) + a is a vertical shift; y = f(x − a) is a horizontal shift the opposite way; y = −f(x) reflects in the x-axis; y = f(−x) reflects in the y-axis; y = af(x) stretches parallel to the y-axis.
tips: The tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.

strands.name: Ratio, proportion & rates of change
strands.note: Joint-largest strand at Foundation. Beyond simple sharing, the marks are in algebraic proportion, compound measures and multi-step best-buy / recipe questions.

subtopics.title: Simplify, share & combine ratios; difference problems
subtopics.method: Simplify by dividing by the HCF: 18 : 24 = 3 : 4. To share an amount in a ratio a : b, find a + b parts, then one part = total ÷ (a + b). For a difference ('A has £12 more than B'), let the parts be 3x and 2x, then 3x − 2x = 12. Combining ratios: if A : B = 2 : 3 and B : C = 4 : 5, make the B parts equal (12) so A : B : C = 8 : 12 : 15.

subtopics.title: Direct proportion (including y = kx²)
subtopics.method: Find k from one pair of values, then use it. Direct-proportion graphs are straight lines through the origin. y ∝ x², y ∝ √x and other powers follow the same 'find k' method.

subtopics.title: Inverse proportion
formulae: y ∝ 1/x → y = k/x, or xy = k
subtopics.method: If one quantity doubles, the other halves. Graphs are reciprocal curves. Worded clues: 'constant product', 'more workers, less time'.

subtopics.title: Percentage change in context; successive percentages
subtopics.method: Best-buy and successive-change questions: apply one multiplier after another. A 10% increase followed by a 10% decrease is × 1.10 × 0.90 = × 0.99, not back to the start. Compound growth uses the power formula; exponential decay (half-life wording) is the same structure with a multiplier less than 1.

subtopics.title: Compound measures: speed, density, pressure
subtopics.method: Rearrange with a formula triangle. Units must match: convert minutes to hours, cm³ to m³, before substituting. Most compound-measure marks are lost on units, not the formula — write the converted values on the page first. 45 minutes is 0.75 hours, not 0.45. 500 m is 0.5 km.

subtopics.title: Distance–time and velocity–time graphs
subtopics.method: Distance–time graphs: gradient = speed; horizontal = stationary; steeper = faster. Velocity–time graphs: gradient = acceleration; area under the line = distance.

subtopics.title: Similar shapes: length, area & volume scale factors
subtopics.method: Similar shapes have equal angles and proportional sides. Ratios of areas and volumes of similar shapes use the square and cube of the length scale factor.

strands.name: Geometry & measures
strands.note: Marks come from diagrams. Redraw if the printed one is cramped. Mark every equal angle, parallel line and given length. Name the rule you use — communication is AO2.

subtopics.title: Angle facts: lines, points, triangles, parallels, polygons
formulae: Interior angle of a regular n-gon = ((n − 2) × 180°) / n
subtopics.method: Angles on a straight line sum to 180°; around a point sum to 360°; vertically opposite angles are equal. Triangle = 180°, quadrilateral = 360°, equilateral all 60°, isosceles base angles equal. Parallel lines: corresponding angles equal, alternate angles equal, co-interior (allied) angles sum to 180°. State the rule you use by name.

subtopics.title: Area & perimeter (compound shapes, trapezium)
formulae: Area of triangle = ½ × base × height
Area of parallelogram = base × perpendicular height
Area of trapezium = ½ (a + b) h
subtopics.method: Split compound shapes into known rectangles and triangles, work out each part, then add or subtract. Keep units consistent.

subtopics.title: Circles: circumference, area, arcs, sectors
subtopics.method: Leave answers in terms of π unless told otherwise — that is an exact-value instruction. A segment is the area between a chord and the arc: sector area minus the triangle.

subtopics.title: Volume & surface area: prisms, cylinders, cones, spheres, pyramids
formulae: Volume of prism = area of cross-section × length
Volume of cylinder = πr²h · Curved SA = 2πrh
Volume of pyramid = ⅓ × base area × height
Volume of cone = ⅓πr²h · Curved SA = πrl
Volume of sphere = 4⁄3 πr³ · Surface area = 4πr²
subtopics.method: Identify the solid, pick the formula, substitute carefully and keep units consistent (a volume is cm³, a surface area is cm²).

subtopics.title: Pythagoras in 2D (and 3D if Higher)
formulae: a² + b² = c²  (c is the hypotenuse)
subtopics.method: Use Pythagoras for right-angled triangles when you have two sides and want the third. c is always the hypotenuse (opposite the right angle). 3D Pythagoras [H / top F]: find a face diagonal first, then the space diagonal.

subtopics.title: Right-angled trigonometry (SOH CAH TOA) & exact values
subtopics.method: Label Opposite, Adjacent and Hypotenuse from the angle you are using. Choose the ratio that uses the two sides you have or want, substitute, then rearrange. Use inverse sin/cos/tan to find an angle. On non-calculator papers use exact values.
tips: Exact values: sin 30=½, cos 60=½, sin/cos 45=√2/2, sin 60=cos 30=√3/2, tan 45=1, tan 30=1/√3, tan 60=√3.

subtopics.title: Transformations: translate, rotate, reflect, enlarge
subtopics.method: Describe fully: translation (vector); rotation (centre, angle, direction); reflection (mirror line); enlargement (centre and scale factor). A missing centre loses the mark. Negative scale factors [H] rotate 180° as well as enlarge.

subtopics.title: Congruence & similarity
formulae: Length k · Area k² · Volume k³
subtopics.method: Congruent triangles: SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS (SSA is not a congruence rule). Similar shapes have equal angles and proportional sides; scale lengths by k, areas by k², volumes by k³.

subtopics.title: Bearings, constructions, loci, unit conversions
formulae: 1 kg = 1000 g · 1 litre = 1000 cm³ · 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³
subtopics.method: Constructions use ruler and compasses only: perpendicular bisector, angle bisector, perpendicular from/to a point on a line, equilateral triangle, 60° and 90°. A locus is the set of points satisfying a rule (all points 4 cm from a point = a circle). Bearings are three-figure angles measured clockwise from North; the back bearing differs by 180°.
tips: Do not mix 12-hour clock notation into calculations.

subtopics.title: Vectors: column vectors, resultant, magnitude
subtopics.method: A vector has magnitude and direction. A column vector (a above b) means a right and b up. Addition is 'follow the path'. Parallel vectors are scalar multiples.
tips: Vector proof [H]: show one vector is a scalar multiple of another sharing a point to prove collinearity.

subtopics.title: Sine & cosine rules; ½ab sin C; circle theorems; vector proof
formulae: Sine rule: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C
Cosine rule: a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A
Area of triangle = ½ ab sin C
subtopics.method: Sine rule: when you have a side and its opposite angle, plus one more side or angle (watch the ambiguous case when finding an angle). Cosine rule: two sides and the included angle (to find the third side), or all three sides (to find an angle). Area = ½ ab sin C with two sides and the included angle. State circle theorems by name as your reason.
tips: Circle theorems: angle in a semicircle = 90°; angle at the centre = twice the angle at the circumference; angles in the same segment are equal; opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°; tangent ⊥ radius; two tangents from a point are equal; alternate segment theorem; the perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects it.

strands.name: Probability & statistics
strands.note: Often underestimated — easy marks if practised. A calculation without a sentence in context often loses the final mark.

subtopics.title: Single-event probability; expected & relative frequency
formulae: P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ equally likely outcomes
Expected frequency = probability × number of trials
subtopics.method: Probability is a number from 0 to 1 inclusive; write it as a fraction in simplest form unless a decimal or percentage is asked. The probabilities of all mutually exclusive outcomes sum to 1. Relative frequency estimates probability and improves with more trials.

subtopics.title: Mutually exclusive & independent events
formulae: Mutually exclusive: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)
Independent: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)
subtopics.method: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together — add. Independent events do not affect each other — multiply. If events are not independent, use conditional values on the second branch of a tree.

subtopics.title: Tree diagrams (including without replacement)
subtopics.method: Write a probability on every branch. Multiply along a path; add different paths that give the same overall event. Without-replacement (dependent) questions change the second-branch fractions — write the new denominators, that is the key step. Check every pair of second branches sums to 1.

subtopics.title: Venn diagrams & set notation
formulae: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
subtopics.method: ξ is the universal set; ∩ is intersection (AND); ∪ is union (OR); A′ is the complement (NOT A). Fill the overlap first.

subtopics.title: Mean, median, mode & range (lists and tables)
formulae: Mean from a frequency table = Σfx ÷ Σf
subtopics.method: Mean = total ÷ number of values. Median = the middle value once ordered (or the midpoint of the two middle values); from a table, find the position and walk the cumulative frequency. Mode = most common value or modal class. Range measures spread, not an average. Outliers pull the mean and the range; the median is more resistant.

subtopics.title: Bar charts, pie charts, pictograms, time series, scatter graphs
subtopics.method: Bar charts (with gaps) for categories; pictograms need a key. Scatter graphs: describe correlation as strong/weak and positive/negative, then interpret in context ('as revision hours increase, scores tend to increase'). Draw a line of best fit through the data cloud; do not extrapolate far beyond the data.

subtopics.title: Conditional probability; histograms
subtopics.method: Histograms (grouped continuous data): the area of each bar is the frequency. Conditional probability: restrict the sample space to B, then look at the overlap; in two-way tables, restrict to the given row or column.

subtopics.title: Cumulative frequency; box plots; comparing distributions
subtopics.method: Cumulative frequency: plot at the upper class boundary; median is the reading at n/2; LQ and UQ at 25% and 75%. Box plots show min, LQ, median, UQ, max. To compare distributions, comment on a measure of average and a measure of spread — in context.
tips: Sampling: a sample should be representative; random sampling gives every member a chance; larger samples are more reliable but costlier; bias comes from a poor sampling frame or a leading question.
